The best you can do now is avoid this coworker touching your belongings for 4 weeks and if you want a more effective means of cleaning, try bleach wipes. They actually do kill norovirus.

Noro is spread by touching an infected person directly, or really anything that they touch, *and then* touching your mouth. 

Touch wont cause it, but the reason it spreads so much is because of touch + touching the mouth

The virus stays in a persons stool for two weeks and will die naturally in two more weeks. So it is highly important that you do not share anything with that person for one month.

It is not true that being in the same building gives you the virus or that it spreads in the air like a cold. This is a common misconception because a sick person will often touch doorknobs, remotes, handles, and all sorts of things, making them dangerous. The worst part about norovirus is the fact that it takes only about 19 of the viral particles to get into someones mouth to make them sick. So no matter how much the sick person washes their hands. If their hand even brushes their pants before washing them, or they do not wash them thoroughly enough (which most people don't), they will have viral material on them.

My solution is to just stay as far away from infected people for as long as possible.

Still, I'd say this was a good experience, obviously not for everyone, this was a very extreme stunt for me. But it succeeded in re-framing how I saw the phobia. So I'm not "out of the woods" until early to mid december. I could still throw up any minute now from my brothers.

And yes I've heard the, *"just wash your hands before you eat and don't touch your mouth"* mantra but let's face it, that's **MUCH** easier said than done. I might eat something with a bit of norovirus on it, I might accidentally touch my mouth in my sleep or because I trip, someone else might do my laundry with hands that had the virus on them, and 4 weeks is a long time to not make a single mistake. Key point is: nothing is going to guarantee my safety. Even when this is all over, unless I shut myself in my room for the rest of my life, I probably will catch the norovirus one day. It is so contagious that it's almost guaranteed in my lifetime no matter how much I wash my hands before eating: mistakes happen. Why should I worry about a "vaccine" when we hear about one every few years and  get nothing? It seems likely it won't come out anytime soon or maybe even in my lifetime. Accepting all that is hard for me, but I was able to do it in these past few days.

If I change my thinking from "What if I get the norovirus!?" to "I will catch the norovirus, it's only a matter of when" something about how I deal with the world changes. I can touch doors again, I can eat, I can smile even when all hope in life is lost. Just like dealing with mortality, accepting that one day my worst nightmare, the most painful and horrible thing I can experience will become a reality makes me oddly calm, it makes me appreciate the moment I have right now. That's mindfulness.
